subject: Cognitive Science
title: Network Effects
description: A fast breakdown of Network Effects for builders.

hook.text: The first fax machine was useless. The second made both valuable. By a million, they changed business.

buildup.text: A network effect means a product gets more valuable as more people use it. Value grows with adoption.

discovery.text: Metcalfe's law says a network's value scales with the square of its users. Two people: one link. Ten: forty-five.

twist.text: Network effects create winner-take-all markets. Once a network leads, it's nearly impossible to overtake.

climax.text: Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb all won through network effects, not through better technology alone.

punchline.text: Value isn't in the product. It's in the network.

quiz.question: What is a network effect?
options: A product becomes more valuable as more people use it
Networks always lose value over time

details.summary: Network effects occur when a product becomes more valuable as more people use it. Telephones, social media, and languages all exhibit this: each new user increases the value for every existing user. Network effects create powerful winner-take-all dynamics in markets.
details.whyItMatters: Network effects explain why dominant platforms are so hard to displace and why early adoption advantages compound over time.
takeaways: Each new user increases value for all existing users
Network effects create winner-take-all market dynamics
Critical mass is the tipping point where growth self-sustains

faq.question: What is the difference between network effects and scale?
faq.answer: Scale means you get cheaper as you grow. Network effects mean you get better as you grow. A factory has economies of scale. A social network has network effects. Scale advantages are linear; network effects are exponential. Both create competitive moats but through different mechanisms.

faq.question: Can network effects work in reverse?
faq.answer: Yes. When users leave, the platform becomes less valuable for remaining users, triggering more departures. This negative network effect can cause rapid collapse once a tipping point is reached. MySpace and early social networks demonstrated how quickly networks can unravel.
